newsitem.title: PERU: Marxist rebels were also religious, hostage says.
newsitem.headline: Marxist rebels were also religious, hostage says.

text.p: Despite their avowed Marxist ideals, many of the Tupac Amaru rebels who seized the Japanese ambassador's home for 126 days were religious and even asked a priest to bring them rosary beads, a hostage said on Saturday.
Father Juan Julio Wicht, a Jesuit priest and one of the 71 hostages freed in a military raid on Tuesday, said he often asked the guerrillas to pray for a safe ending to the siege.
When he gave rosary beads to the hostages, some guerrillas asked if they could have some too, he said. Roman Catholics often hold beads and a crucifix while praying in an act of veneration.

"When I brought the hostages rosary beads, many of them asked, 'Father, could you give me one as well?' I told them to behave well and pray because God was for everyone," Wicht said in an interview on local radio broadcaster CPN.

Wicht, who spent 126 days as a hostage, provided a clearer picture of the 14 rebels who captured world attention before they were killed in the raid. He said a religious feeling existed among them but they had little religious education.

"Good Friday was impressive. They (MRTA) always sang their (rebel) anthems, but on Good Friday there was total silence," Wicht said. "On this day there were no anthems, no hymns. It was their decision."
He said the rebels had never spoken to a priest before.
"They told me, 'So you're a priest. It's the first time I've spoken to a priest.'"
Most of the 14 guerrilla hostage-takers were very young, with very little education, and some were illiterate, he said.

"I had difficulties understanding their Spanish," he said, because of their lack of education and their eastern Peruvian jungle accent. People from that region are known for their slurred, lilting drawl.
One hostage and two Peruvian commandos also died during the storming of the embassy residence.
